title: Satan in the Garden
setting: Mount Niphates, then the garden of Eden from afternoon to night
summary: Satan, torn by despair on Mount Niphates, resolves on evil, then leaps the wall of Paradise and watches Adam and Eve in their happiness, learning of the forbidden tree. Uriel warns Gabriel, whose angels find Satan crouched at Eve’s ear as she sleeps. Satan and Gabriel nearly come to blows until God hangs out his golden scales, and Satan flees.

sections.title: The Hell within him
sections.note: The poet wishes Adam and Eve could have been warned. Satan, nearing his goal, finds no joy in it: he carries Hell inside him wherever he goes.

sections.title: Satan’s soliloquy on Niphates
sections.note: Addressing the sun, Satan admits God deserved no rebellion and that he fell freely. He asks if repentance is possible, decides pride would never let it last, and ends: ‘Evil, be thou my good.’

sections.title: Uriel watches; the borders of Paradise
sections.note: The passions on Satan’s face give him away to Uriel, still watching from the sun. Satan reaches the green, steep wall of Paradise, where the scented air delights even him.

sections.title: Satan leaps the wall
sections.note: Scorning the one gate, Satan vaults the wall like a wolf into a fold and perches on the Tree of Life like a cormorant, using it only as a lookout.

sections.title: The garden described
sections.note: The narrator lays out Paradise: the two trees, the river, the brooks running nectar, flowers poured out by Nature rather than Art. It surpasses every garden of classical legend.

sections.title: Adam and Eve first seen
sections.note: Satan sees the human pair, naked, upright and in God’s image, walking hand in hand among the playful animals. Milton describes their bodies, their unashamed innocence and their supper by a fountain.

sections.title: Satan’s pity and resolve
sections.note: Satan admits he could love these creatures and pities them, yet resolves to destroy them anyway, pleading ‘necessity, the tyrant’s plea.’ He prowls near them as a lion and a tiger.

sections.title: Adam and Eve talk; Eve remembers her waking
sections.note: Adam reminds Eve of their one easy command, not to eat from the tree of knowledge. Eve recalls waking after her creation, falling in love with her own reflection in a pool, and being led by a voice to Adam.

sections.title: Satan’s envy and plan
sections.note: Tormented by their embrace, Satan seizes on what he has overheard: forbidden knowledge. He will stir in them the desire to know and be like gods, and goes off to spy out the garden.

sections.title: Uriel warns Gabriel; evening falls
sections.note: Uriel rides a sunbeam to Gabriel at the eastern gate and warns him of the suspicious spirit. Twilight and the nightingale bring on a moonlit night.

sections.title: Adam and Eve’s evening talk
sections.note: Adam speaks of rest and tomorrow’s work. Eve answers with a love lyric that lists the day’s delights and then repeats them, none sweet without him, and asks why the stars shine all night.

sections.title: The bower and wedded love
sections.note: The couple pray together under the open sky and go to their flowered bower, where they make love. The narrator breaks into a hymn to married love against those who call it impure.

sections.title: Satan found at Eve’s ear
sections.note: Gabriel sends out the night watch and dispatches Ithuriel and Zephon to the bower. They find Satan squatting like a toad by sleeping Eve, working on her dreams; Ithuriel’s spear touches him and he springs up in his own shape.

sections.title: Satan rebuked by Zephon
sections.note: Satan sneers that the angels should know him; Zephon replies that his brightness is gone with his goodness. Satan feels ‘how awful goodness is’ and is led, champing like a reined horse, to Gabriel.

sections.title: Satan and Gabriel
sections.note: Gabriel demands why Satan has broken out of Hell. They trade taunts, Gabriel exposing each of Satan’s shifting excuses and threatening to drag him back in chains.

sections.title: The golden scales
sections.note: The angels close in and Satan swells to the size of a mountain, but before they fight God hangs out his scales in the sky. Gabriel shows Satan his side weighs light, and Satan flees with the night.

glosses.note: The Book of Revelation. Its author hears a voice cry ‘Woe to the inhabiters of the earth’ when the Dragon is cast down (Revelation 12:12).
The Hebrew name Satan means adversary or accuser; Revelation calls him ‘the accuser of our brethren.’ Here he comes first as tempter.

famous.why: ‘Which way I fly is Hell; myself am Hell’ answers Satan’s own boast in Book 1 that the mind is its own place.
‘Evil, be thou my good’ is the moment Satan chooses evil with open eyes.
The first sight of Adam and Eve, ‘godlike erect,’ includes the much-debated line ‘He for God only, she for God in him.’
Eve’s ‘Sweet is the breath of Morn’ lists the day’s pleasures, then repeats every one to say none is sweet without Adam.
‘Hail, wedded Love’ is Milton’s bold hymn to married sex as part of innocent life in Paradise.
Satan found ‘squat like a toad, close at the ear of Eve’ is the poem’s most deflating image of him.

themes: Satan’s soliloquy shows he knows the truth and chooses evil anyway; Hell is a state of mind he cannot leave.
Paradise is a working garden of abundance, where innocence includes love, labour and sex.
The order between Adam and Eve is presented as harmonious, but Eve’s mirror scene hints at her separate inner life.
Goodness has its own power: Satan is undone less by force than by beauty, rebuke and God’s scales.
art: Satan crouched like a toad at the ear of sleeping Eve in the flowered bower, as the young angel Ithuriel reaches out with his spear to touch him.
